title: Giri Beats Abdusattorov As Bayegan Pendik Wins European Club Cup
summary: GM Anish Giri scored a crushing win over GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov as top-seed Bayegan Pendik Chess Sports Club beat defending champion SuperChess Romania 3.5-2.5 to win the 2026 European Chess Club Cup. Novy Bor Chess Club missed out on gold on tiebreaks despite overpowering Elektroprivreda 4.5-1.5, while GM Boris Gelfand-led Rishon LeZion A snatched bronze by winning the battle of the underdogs against Cheddleton Savills Catering 5.5-0.5. Defending champion Cercle d'Echecs de Monte-Carlo clinched the 2026 European Women's Chess Club Cup after a 4-0 win in the final round helped them finish above CE Gambit Bonnevoie on tiebreaks, with Monte-Carlo also claiming individual gold on boards one (GM Aleksandra Goryachkina), two (GM Koneru Humpy), and four (GM Elisabeth Paehtz). Sirmium Sremska Mitrovica took bronze after a 3.5-0.5 victory over the round-six heroes, Odlar Yurdu. Meanwhile, 11-year-old FM Bodhana Sivanandan won on demand to score her final IM norm and become the seventh youngest IM of all time—a feat we've covered in this separate report. Bayegan Pendik Chess Sports Club surprisingly easily won the battle of the leaders against SuperChess Romania, but looked on nervously as Novy Bor Chess Club racked up a big score to beat Elektroprivreda—the margin of the win could matter for tiebreaks. In the end, however, Bayegan Pendik took gold by 8.5 tiebreak points. Rishon LeZion A, who won all their matches except for a loss to Novy Bor in round four, took bronze, while SuperChess Romania still earned a spot in the 2027 European Chess Super League. title: Bodhana, 11, Breaks Judit Polgar’s Record To Become Youngest Female IM In History
summary: The extraordinary FM Bodhana Sivanandan has done it again. On Friday, the 11-year-old prodigy achieved yet another record, becoming the youngest girl ever to complete the requirements for the International Master title, securing her third and final norm at the European Club Cup in Budva, Montenegro. Bodhana defeated WIM Viktoria Johansson of Sweden's Wasa SK in the seventh and final round, finishing on 5.5/7 on board one for her team, She Plays To Win Lionesses A. With a rating performance of 2465, she achieved her third and final IM norm. At 11 years, seven months, and 16 days, that means she has broken a female age record held by GM Judit Polgar since 1988. The Hungarian earned the IM title at 12, before going on to become the strongest female player in chess history. Congratulations to 11-year-old IM Bodhana Sivanandan on scoring her final IM norm to become the 7th youngest IM in chess history — and the youngest female IM ever! https://t.co/odYTIrc3Qn https://t.co/gqWP8GkCcg In a post-game interview with WCM Tallulah Roberts on the official broadcast, Bodhana, when asked about the achievement, said she was already looking toward her next goal. "I'm happy about that but hopefully I'm able to get grandmaster soon as well!" she said. I'm happy about that but hopefully I'm able to get grandmaster soon as well!—Bodhana Sivanandan The British prodigy from Harrow outside London has not only broken a record Polgar held for 38 years, but she is also the seventh-youngest player of all time to qualify for the title, according to Chess.com's research. She is exactly one month older than World Championship Challenger GM Javokhir Sindarov was when he achieved his IM title in 2017, while the reigning champion GM Gukesh Dommaraju was almost two months older in 2018. She is one of only ten players to complete the title before turning 12. "You can only describe her as a generational talent, I am delighted that it's happening," IM Malcolm Pein, Director of International Chess and External Relations at the English Chess Federation, told Chess.com. "I think we stopped being surprised by her achievements in the last year." The achievement comes less than a month after she became the youngest player ever to fulfill the requirements for the Woman Grandmaster (WGM) title at the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. While still awaiting formal approval for that title, she has now passed the required 2400 live rating during the European Club Cup, and also completed the requirements for the higher, open IM title, which is available to players of any gender. Playing on board one for She Plays To Win Lionesses A, Sivanandan recovered from an opening-round defeat against former Women's World Championship challenger GM Aleksandra Goryachkina. She struck back with two wins, including this one over IM Olga Badelka.

title: Magnus Carlsen Headlines New Barcelona Rapid Event With 1-Second Increment
summary: GM Magnus Carlsen wants more events that are exciting to watch. Now he has helped shape one. The world number-one will headline the inaugural MOVE Cup in Barcelona on January 19–20, 2027, an eight-player rapid tournament with €300,000 in prizes and a one-second increment intended to keep the pressure on. The two-day event is backed by sportsbook technology supplier BETBY, which has sponsored Carlsen since 2024. A charity hand-and-brain event on January 18 will precede the main competition, which takes place alongside ICE Barcelona, a trade show for the gaming industry. Organizers said the tournament is guaranteed to take place in Barcelona for the next three years. Carlsen is the only confirmed participant, but the remaining seven grandmasters, expected to be some of the top names in the world, will be announced in the coming weeks. “The fact that Magnus Carlsen is involved speaks for itself," eight-time Spanish chess champion GM Miguel Illescas said at a press conference in Barcelona on October 20. Carlsen noted how chess has grown in recent years, but argued he wants events that can attract more fans. "I think we kind of lack events that bring chess to an audience that can have a better spectator experience that makes it more exciting," he said. We lack events that bring chess to an audience that can have a better spectator experience that makes it more exciting.—Magnus Carlsen At the MOVE Cup, spectators on site will be able to follow live commentary through headphones, with scores displayed on large screens, similar to Chess.com's Speed Chess Championship Finals and the Esports World Cup Final. Magnus Carlsen discussing the format of the Move Cup during yesterday’s press conference. https://t.co/jhXT4EkHe1 "This will be a lot of fun and really exciting to follow," Carlsen said. The world number-one has played a part in designing the tournament format. Games will be played with 10 minutes plus a one-second increment. "One second is just about enough to physically make the moves," he explained. “Two seconds, the problem is that you can accumulate time," he said, suggesting a 1.5-second increment would be ideal. One second is just about enough to physically make the moves. Two seconds, the problem is that you can accumulate time.—Magnus Carlsen The first day consists of a round-robin with the eight players, with the top four players advancing to semifinals. The knockout phase will be played as best of three games, while the final will be best of five games. The launch also introduces the MOVE Foundation, which will receive a €300,000 contribution matching the players’ prize fund. Organizers say any additional money raised during the tournament will be divided equally between the prize fund and the foundation. The foundation’s stated priorities include chess development, support for young talent, and research into chess and mental health. Board member Inese Dabola said it would work with existing projects as well as develop its own programs, with information about donations and activities published online. "We believe chess has a lot to offer today," Dabola said. It's worth noting that the MOVE Cup overlaps with Tata Steel Chess, a tournament that has been on the chess calendar for decades. In 2027, it runs from January 15-31 in Wijk aan Zee, the Netherlands. Carlsen has won the Dutch tournament eight times, but has not played there since 2023. Asked by Chess.com about the clash, he smiled: "It means that I’m not playing next year," adding that he has a great relationship with the Dutch organizers. "On a more general point, it would of course be good if there was more coordination in the chess world and that it were less fragmented. But it is what it is." For Carlsen, the MOVE Cup marks yet another speed chess tournament on his calendar. A highlight of the press conference was Illescas, who worked with former World Champion GM Vladimir Kramnik, asking whether Carlsen would consider returning to the World Championship cycle for $20 million. "Most people have a price, obviously," Carlsen said. "But I am not going to speculate what that price is. From a sporting perspective, there are a lot of things in chess that interest me more than a classical match."
